newsitem.title: MONGOLIA: Mongolians mark Buddhist revival with huge statue.
newsitem.headline: Mongolians mark Buddhist revival with huge statue.

text.p: Thousands of Mongolians converged on Ulan Bator on Sunday for the unveiling of a giant Buddhist statue made to replace one that vanished in religious purges inspired by Josef Stalin almost 60 years ago.

Throngs of people, many wearing colourful traditional dress, crowded the Gandan monastery in the Mongolian capital for a close-up view of the 26-metre (85-foot), gold-plated monument to the country's Buddhist revival.
Crimson-clad monks danced and chanted prayers in the public dedication of the statue.

The original sculpture, commissioned by Mongolia's last khan (ruler) in 1911, disappeared in 1938 during a brutal purge of the nation's monasteries in which thousands of monks were killed and their temples were destroyed.
Many Mongolians believe the original was hacked to pieces and shipped to what was then the Soviet Union where it was melted down to make bullets.
Mongolian historians estimate a total of 17,000 monks were killed and more than 700 monasteries destroyed during the communist repression of the 1930s and 1940s.
Historians say Stalin's purges in Mongolia were designed to ensure a tight political grip on a buffer state sharing borders with potentially hostile China and Japanese-dominated Manchuria.
President Punsalmaagiin Ochirbat, speaking at the dedication, hailed the statue as "a symbol of Mongolia's unity and independence".
Mongolia's national artist Tsultem said the sculpture had more than just religious significance for the 2.3 million people of this vast nation wedged between Russia and China.
"It has become a symbol of independence. Dedicating it is a matter of national pride for anyone regardless of religion," Tsultem said.

About 50 sculptors and artisans had laboured since 1989 to complete the 90-tonne image of the Buddhist god of mercy, adorning it with 2.6 kg (5.7 lb) of gold and 25 kg (55 lb) of silver as well as precious stones.
The statue's cavernous interior is filled with incense, Buddhist scripture and Mongolian soil.
"We believe (the statue) is brought to life, the same way as we people are alive, after two days of chanting," an elderly monk said.

Buddhism has seen a resurgence in Mongolia since a peaceful revolution in 1990 broke the Soviet-backed Communist Party's monopoly on power. The religious revival followed as Mongolians recreated traditions the communists had tried to uproot.
More than 150 temples and monasteries have been restored and there now are around 2,000 monks in the country, compared with less than 200 six years ago.
But many Mongolians say the flowering of Buddhist culture has been slow as the nation struggles with painful economic reform and as more Mongolians convert to foreign religions.
"Buddhism is not going to grow into the scope it had before the (communist) revolution, at least not soon," said one young monk. "Perhaps one day, far in the future, it may do so."
